cards.back: Hypo + seizures: 3% saline bolus • SIADH: fluid restriction • chronic hypo: ≤8-10 mmol/L/24 h (osmotic demyelination) • hyper: over 48 h, ≤0.5 mmol/L/h (cerebral oedema); 0.9% saline for shock.

I-45.summary: High potassium in a well infant is a haemolysed heel-prick until a free-flowing venous sample proves otherwise; real hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T → wide QRS → sine wave) needs calcium gluconate first to protect the heart, then shift (salbutamol, insulin-glucose) and remove. Low potassium: replace magnesium and never bolus KCl.

questions.stem: What is the commonest cause of a high potassium result in a well infant?
questions.explain: The commonest cause of high K in a well infant is a haemolysed (squeezed heel-prick) sample releasing intracellular potassium. Repeat with a free-flowing venous sample before acting, unless the child is unwell or has ECG changes.
questions.note: Commonest cause of high K in a well infant: a haemolysed sample.

questions.stem: A well, feeding 3-week-old has a routine heel-prick potassium of 7.2 mmol/L. Sodium is normal and he is clinically well. What is the next best step?
options: Repeat on a free-flowing venous sample
questions.explain: First exclude a haemolysed heel-prick by repeating a free-flowing venous sample (with an ECG if any doubt). Treating a spurious result is harmful; calcium is for confirmed hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.
questions.note: First exclude haemolysed heel-prick; repeat free-flowing venous sample.

questions.stem: What is the earliest ECG change of hyperkalaemia?
options: Loss of P waves with a sine-wave pattern
questions.explain: The progression is peaked T waves → loss of P waves/wide QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole. U waves and flat T waves are features of hypokalaemia.
questions.note: Earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia: peaked T waves → wide QRS → sine wave.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with acute kidney injury has K 7.8 mmol/L on a venous sample and the ECG shows broad QRS complexes. What should be given first?
questions.explain: With ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate 10% is given first to stabilise (protect) the myocardium within minutes; it does not lower K. Then shift with salbutamol/insulin-glucose and remove with resin, loop diuretic or dialysis.
questions.note: High with ECG changes: IV calcium gluconate 10% first (protect).

questions.stem: A child with AKI has K 7.6 mmol/L, and another child with pyloric stenosis has K 2.4 mmol/L. Both are at risk of arrhythmia. Which cardiac property, set chiefly by the potassium gradient, explains this?
options: AV nodal conduction via adenosine receptors
The plateau phase driven by calcium influx
Sinus node automaticity via the funny current
questions.explain: K⁺ sets the resting membrane potential; both high and low K⁺ alter it, disturbing excitability and repolarisation. In hyperkalaemia, partial depolarisation inactivates fast Na⁺ channels (slow conduction, wide QRS); salbutamol and insulin then shift K⁺ into cells via Na/K-ATPase.
questions.note: Abnormal K⁺; K⁺ sets the resting membrane potential.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old on long-term furosemide has K 2.6 mmol/L that does not rise despite 48 hours of adequate KCl replacement. Which deficiency is most likely preventing correction?
questions.explain: Low magnesium increases renal potassium wasting (via ROMK channels), so low K may not correct until magnesium is replaced. Loop diuretics cause both.
questions.note: Low K may not correct until magnesium is replaced.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with newly diagnosed DKA has K 5.1 mmol/L at presentation. Six hours after starting an insulin infusion he develops muscle weakness and his ECG shows flat T waves and U waves. What explains this?
questions.explain: Insulin in DKA shifts K into cells and unmasks the total-body K deficit, causing hypokalaemia (weakness, flat T waves, U waves). This is why potassium is added to DKA fluids once urine output is confirmed.
questions.note: Low: diarrhoea and vomiting, pyloric stenosis, diuretics, insulin in DKA, refeeding.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with K 2.8 mmol/L after severe gastroenteritis is vomiting and cannot take oral fluids. The ECG shows U waves but no arrhythmia. What is the most appropriate way to replace potassium?
options: IV KCl as a rapid undiluted bolus
IV KCl diluted in maintenance fluids
Oral KCl only, repeating doses if vomited
questions.explain: Low K is replaced with oral KCl when possible; otherwise IV potassium is added to fluids at a controlled concentration and rate, never as a bolus (risk of cardiac arrest). Check and replace magnesium as well.
questions.note: Low: oral KCl; IV in fluids, never bolus; replace Mg.

cards.front: Walk through the management of hyperkalaemia in a child.
cards.back: Exclude haemolysed sample; ECG • ECG changes: IV calcium gluconate 10% (protect) • shift: salbutamol, insulin-glucose, sodium bicarbonate • remove: resin, loop diuretic, dialysis • stop K-raising drugs.

cards.front: List the causes of hyperkalaemia and hypokalaemia in children.
cards.back: High: haemolysed sample, AKI, CAH, DKA, tumour lysis, ACE inhibitors, heparin, trimethoprim • Low: D&V, pyloric stenosis, diuretics, insulin in DKA, refeeding.

cards.front: Compare the ECG and clinical features of high and low potassium.
cards.back: High: peaked T → wide QRS → sine wave → VF • Low: weakness, ileus, flat T, U waves • work-up of low K: urine K (>20 = renal loss), acid-base, Mg.
